dedupe_keys.name: comparing the impacts of northeast hurricanes on energy infrastructure us doe april 2013 irene and sandy

description: This case study is a 50-page report from the US Department of Energy's Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability, prepared with ICF International in April 2013, that compares how Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Sandy in 2012 affected energy infrastructure in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. It compares the storms, their storm surge and tides, then electricity impacts including power outages, restoration and nuclear power plants, and petroleum impacts including refineries, pipelines and terminals. The executive summary reports that Irene disrupted power to 6.69 million customers and Sandy, with the November 2012 nor'easter, to 8.66 million, that utilities restored 95 percent of customers 10 days after Sandy's peak against 5 days after Irene, and that petroleum product supply through the New York Harbor terminals recovered more slowly after Sandy. Access: the report is a free PDF from the DOE website; no licence is stated. Coverage is the US Northeast and Mid-Atlantic for two storms. Caveats: it is a government comparison of two events, and figures come from utility, EIA and NOAA sources cited in the report. It suits resilience and recovery studies of coastal energy systems, and no directly related records are catalogued yet.

name: Comparing the Impacts of Northeast Hurricanes on Energy Infrastructure (US DOE, April 2013: Irene and Sandy)
outcomes: Sandy affected a larger area and lasted longer than Irene: outages reached 8.66 million customers against 6.69 million, 95 percent of affected customers were restored 10 days after the outage peak against 5 days after Irene, and petroleum infrastructure in the New York Harbor area took longer to restore, with terminal deliveries at 61 percent of pre-storm levels more than 9 days after Sandy.
